name: Classify a text column with an LLM
desc: Label free text into fixed categories with no training data, then quantify it

cells.code:
## 🏷️ Classify a text column with an LLM

Turn a column of free text — support tickets, reviews, feedback — into **structured labels** with no training data and no model to fit. You give the LLM a fixed set of categories and it assigns each row to one (or several). Great for triage, routing, and turning qualitative text into something you can `group_by` and chart.

**Cost model:** this runs **one LLM call per row** (concurrently). So sample large tables first with `.head(...)` while you dial in your labels and instructions, then scale up once you're happy. Set `temperature=0` (the default) for deterministic labels, and use `instructions=` to nudge edge cases (e.g. "treat refund questions as billing").

Returns a tidy DataFrame with `text` + `label` (a list of labels when `multi_label=True`).

# 1) Load the text rows. Sample large tables while iterating — one LLM call per row.
df = read_dynamodb("<your-table>").head(100)
df.head()

# 2) Classify each row into your fixed label set. instructions= steers edge cases;
#    system= sets a persona if you want one. Returns a DataFrame with text + label.
labeled = llm_classify(
    df["<text_column>"],
    labels=["billing", "technical", "account", "other"],
    instructions="Treat refund and payment questions as 'billing'.",
)
labeled.head()

# 3) Quantify it — the point of labeling is to COUNT. Attach the labels back to the
#    source rows and see the category mix at a glance.
df = df.assign(category=labeled["label"].values)
df["category"].value_counts()

# 4) Visualize the distribution (plot_bar is pre-loaded — no import). It takes a
#    DataFrame with x/y columns, so turn the counts into one first.
counts = df["category"].value_counts().rename_axis("category").reset_index(name="count")
plot_bar(counts, x="category", y="count", title="Tickets by category")
